title: Condensed matter
tagline: Why solids are metals, insulators or magnets
summary: Crystal lattices, phonons, the free-electron gas, band structure, semiconductors, and an introduction to magnetism and superconductivity.
overview: A solid is a quantum many-body problem with some $10^{23}$ particles per cubic centimetre. It is tractable at all because a crystal is periodic: its vibrations and its electron states are waves labelled by a wavevector that is defined only up to a vector of the reciprocal lattice, and the whole of the physics can be drawn inside one cell of that lattice, the first Brillouin zone. This course builds that picture from the lattice up and uses it to explain why solids are metals, insulators, semiconductors, magnets or superconductors.

The first chapter fixes the geometry: Bravais lattices, the reciprocal lattice and X-ray diffraction, with Bragg's and Laue's conditions proved equivalent. Lattice vibrations, quantised as phonons, then explain the heat capacity of insulators through the Einstein and Debye models. Electrons are treated first as a free gas, classically with Drude and quantum mechanically with Sommerfeld, and then as Bloch waves in a periodic potential, where gaps open at the zone boundaries and the counting of states separates metals from insulators. Semiconductors apply the band picture to the carrier densities of silicon and to the p–n junction. The last chapter leaves independent electrons behind for ordered states: ferromagnetism from exchange, treated in mean-field theory, and superconductivity from the London equations to the flux quantum and the Josephson effect.

What makes the subject hard is the number of scales in play: ångström lattice constants, electronvolt band energies, millielectronvolt phonons and superconducting gaps, kelvin and thousands of kelvin. The remedy is to estimate. Every chapter computes real numbers for real materials, from the Fermi energy of copper to the intrinsic carrier density of silicon, and checking orders of magnitude is the best way to learn which approximations matter. Draw the Brillouin zone; almost every qualitative question about a solid is a question about the band structure plotted in it.
outcomes: Describe crystals as a Bravais lattice plus a basis, and construct the reciprocal lattice and first Brillouin zone of the cubic lattices.
Prove that the Bragg and Laue diffraction conditions are equivalent, and use structure factors to index a powder pattern and identify fcc and bcc lattices.
Derive the phonon dispersion of monatomic and diatomic chains and the Einstein and Debye heat capacities, including the low-temperature $T^3$ law.
Compute Drude conductivities and Hall coefficients, and Fermi energies, electronic heat capacities and Lorenz numbers in the Sommerfeld model.
Prove Bloch's theorem and derive band gaps in the nearly-free-electron model and bands in the tight-binding model, with effective masses and holes.
Explain from the counting of states why a crystal is a metal or an insulator.
Calculate intrinsic and extrinsic carrier densities in semiconductors using the law of mass action, and the built-in potential, depletion width and current of a p–n junction.
Derive Curie's law and the mean-field theory of ferromagnetism, and explain why exchange rather than dipolar interaction orders a magnet.
Derive the London penetration depth and flux quantisation in units of h/2e, and use the BCS gap relation and the Josephson relations quantitatively.

chapters.title: Crystal lattices
chapters.summary: Bravais lattices, the reciprocal lattice, Bragg and Laue diffraction, and structure factors.

chapters.title: Phonons
chapters.summary: Chains of atoms, acoustic and optical branches, and the Debye model.

chapters.title: The free-electron gas
chapters.summary: The Fermi sphere, the density of states, heat capacity and conductivity.

chapters.title: Band structure
chapters.summary: Bloch’s theorem, the nearly-free-electron model, and metals versus insulators.

chapters.title: Semiconductors
chapters.summary: Electrons and holes, doping, and the p–n junction.

chapters.title: Order
chapters.summary: Dia- and paramagnetism, exchange and mean-field ferromagnetism, and superconductivity from the London equations to BCS, flux quantisation and the Josephson effect.

history.title: Drude's electron gas
history.detail: Paul Drude applied the kinetic theory of gases to the electrons in a metal, explaining Ohm's law and, with a lucky factor of two, the Wiedemann–Franz law.

history.title: The first quantum solid
history.detail: Albert Einstein applied Planck's quantum hypothesis to atomic vibrations and explained why diamond falls below the Dulong–Petit heat capacity. In the same year Pierre Weiss proposed the molecular field of ferromagnets.

history.title: Superconductivity
history.detail: Heike Kamerlingh Onnes found that the resistance of mercury vanishes below about 4.2 K, three years after he first liquefied helium.

history.title: X-ray diffraction and the Debye model
history.detail: Max von Laue proposed that crystals diffract X-rays and Walter Friedrich and Paul Knipping observed it; William Lawrence Bragg reinterpreted the spots as reflections from lattice planes, and with his father determined the first crystal structures in 1913. Peter Debye published his theory of the heat capacity of solids the same year.

history.title: Bloch waves and the Sommerfeld gas
history.detail: Felix Bloch proved that electron states in a periodic potential are modulated plane waves, and Arnold Sommerfeld rebuilt Drude's model on Fermi–Dirac statistics. Werner Heisenberg explained ferromagnetism by exchange in the same year.

history.title: The Meissner effect
history.detail: Walther Meissner and Robert Ochsenfeld found that a superconductor expels a magnetic field; Fritz and Heinz London gave the electrodynamics of the effect in 1935.

history.title: The transistor
history.detail: John Bardeen and Walter Brattain demonstrated the point-contact transistor at Bell Laboratories in December 1947; William Shockley's junction transistor and diode theory followed in 1948–49.

history.title: BCS theory
history.detail: John Bardeen, Leon Cooper and Robert Schrieffer explained superconductivity by the pairing of electrons through the lattice, predicting the energy gap.

history.title: The Josephson effect
history.detail: Brian Josephson predicted that Cooper pairs tunnel between superconductors with a current set by their phase difference, oscillating at 2eV/h under a voltage V; Philip Anderson and John Rowell observed it in 1963.

history.title: High-temperature superconductors
history.detail: Georg Bednorz and Alex Müller found superconductivity near 35 K in a lanthanum–barium–copper oxide; within a year YBa₂Cu₃O₇ was found to superconduct at 93 K, above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen.

references.title: The Oxford Solid State Basics
references.note: The best first book: covers almost exactly this course, with clear derivations of phonons, bands and semiconductors and problems that teach.

references.title: Introduction to Solid State Physics
references.note: Eighth edition. The classic text, and the standard source of tabulated data: Debye temperatures, Fermi energies, susceptibilities and superconducting parameters.

references.title: Solid State Physics
references.authors: Neil W. Ashcroft and N. David Mermin
references.note: Deeper and more careful; the chapters on the Drude and Sommerfeld models, Bloch's theorem and semiclassical dynamics are the standard references for the proofs sketched here.

references.title: Solid-State Physics: An Introduction to Principles of Materials Science
references.note: Fourth edition. Strong on experiment, with good treatments of diffraction, phonon measurements and semiconductors.

references.title: Physics of Semiconductor Devices
references.authors: S. M. Sze and Kwok K. Ng
references.note: Third edition. The engineer's reference for carrier statistics, the p–n junction, transistors and material parameters of silicon and gallium arsenide.

references.title: Magnetism in Condensed Matter
references.note: A readable account of dia-, para- and ferromagnetism, exchange and mean-field theory, at the level just beyond this course.

references.title: Introduction to Superconductivity
references.note: Second edition. The standard text on the London and Ginzburg–Landau theories, BCS, vortices and the Josephson effect.

references.title: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Volume III
references.authors: Richard P. Feynman, Robert B. Leighton and Matthew Sands
references.note: Chapters 13 and 14 on propagation in a crystal lattice and semiconductors, and chapter 21 on superconductivity, are a beautiful informal introduction.
